T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a premium, safety‑focused home cleaning solution that reduces water waste and provides a professional‑grade clean, because they are willing to pay a premium for convenience and environmental benefits.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small‑business owners who value eco‑friendly cleaning and are willing to pay more for a product that delivers professional results.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing environmental awareness and demand for water‑saving cleaning solutions create a willingness to pay a premium for a product that reduces water usage and provides superior cleanliness.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tennant can capture value by pricing the consumer product at a premium, selling through retail channels, and leveraging its brand reputation for professional quality to justify higher prices.
assumptions: Consumers are aware of and value water‑saving cleaning solutions.
The premium price is acceptable to a segment of consumers willing to pay for convenience and environmental benefits.
Retail distribution can effectively reach the target consumer base.
predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced consumer version of a professional floor scrubber, at least 30% of surveyed consumers will express intent to purchase or pre‑order within 12 weeks.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Time constraints and lack of technical skills make consumers prefer products that are simple to use and require minimal training, leading them to choose a product that integrates seamlessly into their daily routine.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tennant can capture value by offering a consumer product with intuitive design, easy operation, and minimal maintenance, and by selling through retail channels that cater to busy consumers.
assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience and ease of use over advanced features.

predictions: In a test offering a consumer version of a professional floor scrubber with a simplified interface and low‑training requirements, at least 25% of surveyed consumers will express intent to purchase or pre‑order within 12 weeks.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product descriptions of a consumer version of a professional floor scrubber. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a premium‑priced description emphasizing water‑saving and professional‑grade clean (T1) or a convenience‑focused description emphasizing simple operation and low‑training requirements (T2). After viewing the description, participants indicate purchase intent (yes‑no) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 400 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and household income to reflect the target consumer segment.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes‑no) and maximum price participants would pay, and the proportion of participants who select each attribute (premium‑priced vs. convenience‑focused).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% of participants will select the premium‑priced description and indicate purchase intent, with the convenience‑focused description receiving less than 20% of responses.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 25% of participants will select the convenience‑focused description and indicate purchase intent, with the premium‑priced description receiving less than 20% of responses.

X1.decision_rule: If the premium‑priced description receives at least 30% of purchase intent and the convenience‑focused description receives less than 20%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition based on premium positioning (support T1). If the convenience‑focused description receives at least 25% of purchase intent and the premium‑priced description receives less than 20%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition based on convenience positioning (support T2). If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the product as a premium, water‑saving, professional‑grade home cleaning solution. final.target_customer: Homeowners and small‑business owners in the United States who value eco‑friendly cleaning and are willing to pay a premium for professional‑grade results.
final.value_proposition: A consumer version of a professional floor scrubber that delivers superior cleanliness, reduces water usage, and leverages Tennant’s professional brand reputation, offering a premium price point that reflects the product’s performance and
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test (400 U.S. adults, 12‑week timeline, €20,000 budget) to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity under premium‑priced versus convenience‑focused positioning.
final.uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay a premium for water‑saving features and the size of the consumer market remain uncertain. Evidence from the test will determine whether demand justifies investment.
would_change_if: If the premium‑priced description does not achieve at least 30% purchase intent and the convenience‑focused description does not achieve at least 25%, the investment would be reconsidered in favor of no expansion.
If new public evidence shows strong consumer demand for low‑maintenance, easy‑to‑use home cleaning solutions, the recommendation would shift toward convenience positioning.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Tennant Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional floor-cleaning machines.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered from public sources.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage that would generate value for Tennant.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., residential home cleaning, small‑business cleaning, or a niche professional segment).
2) Expand the existing professional product line with new features or packaging without creating a separate consumer brand (e.g., premium branding, new accessories).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current professional market and existing distribution channels.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce, subscription model, or partnership with retail chains) without altering the product.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from generic cleaning tools to specialized products when they experience a clear benefit (e.g., faster cleaning, reduced water usage, or ease of use) that addresses a specific pain point.

assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for convenience and sustainability.
Tennant can effectively communicate the specific benefits of its products to consumers.
The market size for home cleaning equipment is large enough to support a differentiated proposition.
predictions: In a test offering a premium-priced, feature-rich consumer scrubber, purchase intent will be at least 20% higher than for a standard professional model.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Tennant can capture value through premium pricing justified by safety certifications, direct-to-consumer sales, and brand positioning as a trusted, safe cleaning solution.
assumptions: Consumers prioritize safety and reliability over price in home cleaning equipment.
Tennant can obtain or communicate safety certifications that differentiate its products.
The market size for safety-focused home cleaning equipment is large enough to support a differentiated proposition.
predictions: In a test offering a safety-certified consumer scrubber, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than for a standard professional model.

Begin with a limited retail launch in regions with high environmental awareness to test demand before broader rollout.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Tennant Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional floor-cleaning machines.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered from public sources.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage that would generate value for Tennant.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., residential home cleaning, small‑business cleaning, or a niche professional segment).
2) Expand the existing professional product line with new features or packaging without creating a separate consumer brand (e.g., premium branding, new accessories).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current professional market and existing distribution channels.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce, subscription model, or partnership with retail chains) without altering the product.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a premium, safety‑focused home cleaning solution that reduces water waste and provides a higher level of clean, because they are willing to pay a premium for convenience and environmental benefits.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small‑business owners who value water‑saving and high‑cleanliness for hard‑floor surfaces.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing environmental awareness and awareness of water usage in household cleaning drives consumers to choose products that reduce water consumption and provide superior cleaning performance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tennant can capture value by pricing the consumer product at a premium, selling through retail channels, and leveraging its brand reputation for professional quality to justify higher prices.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for water‑saving and high‑cleanliness features.
Retail distribution can reach target consumers effectively.
The product can be produced at a cost that allows a premium price without eroding margins.
predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced consumer version of a professional floor scrubber, at least 30% of surveyed consumers will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales conversion rate will be higher in regions with higher environmental awareness scores compared to regions with lower awareness.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Modern consumers prioritize convenience and ease of use; a product that requires minimal training and operation aligns with their desire for quick, hassle‑free solutions.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tennant can capture value by offering a consumer product with simplified controls, compact design, and easy storage, and by selling through retail channels that cater to busy consumers.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that reduces setup and operation time.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with a randomized between‑subjects design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A (premium‑priced water‑saving version) and Condition B (premium‑priced convenience‑focused version). Each condition presents a mock product description of a professional floor scrubber, highlighting either water‑saving features or convenience and low‑maintenance features. Participants are then asked to indicate their willingness to pay a premium (maximum price they would pay) and to report purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested).
X1.sample: 500 adult consumers in the United States, recruited via an online panel, balanced across both conditions (250 per condition).
X1.measure: Willingness to pay premium (maximum price) and purchase intent (7‑point scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will show higher willingness to pay premium and higher purchase intent than Condition B because participants prioritize water‑saving features.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will show higher willingness to pay premium and higher purchase intent than Condition A because participants prioritize convenience and low‑maintenance features.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay premium in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., Condition A: 45% vs Condition B: 35%), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on water‑saving features. If Condition B exceeds Condition A by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience and low‑maintenance features. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, indicate uncertainty and recommend further market research.

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer willingness to pay for water‑saving features, so it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes water‑saving and high‑cleanliness features, targeting environmentally conscious homeowners and small‑business owners. Begin with a limited retail launch in regions with high environmental awareness to test demand before broader rollout.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and small‑business owners who value water‑saving and high‑cleanliness for hard‑floor surfaces.
final.value_proposition: A premium‑priced consumer version of a professional floor scrubber that delivers superior cleaning performance while reducing water usage, leveraging Tennant’s professional brand reputation to justify higher prices.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test (500 U.S. adults, 10‑week timeline, €18,000 budget) to measure willingness to pay premium and purchase intent for water‑saving versus convenience‑focused versions.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the exact willingness to pay for water‑saving features are unknown. The test will resolve whether consumers prioritize environmental benefits or convenience.
would_change_if: If the test shows a willingness to pay premium difference of less than 10 percentage points between water‑saving and convenience versions, indicating insufficient demand to justify investment.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for convenience and low‑maintenance features, shifting the recommendation toward a convenience‑focused proposition.

arguments.name: Consumer Proposition Preference Test
arguments.method: Online survey with a randomized between‑subjects design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A (premium‑priced water‑saving version) and Condition B (premium‑priced convenience‑focused version). Each condition presents a mock product description of a professional floor scrubber, highlighting either water‑saving features or convenience and low‑maintenance features. Participants are then asked to indicate their willingness to pay a premium (maximum price they would pay) and to report purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested).
arguments.sample: 500 adult consumers in the United States, recruited via an online panel, balanced across both conditions (250 per condition).
arguments.measure: Willingness to pay premium (maximum price) and purchase intent (7‑point scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will show higher willingness to pay premium and higher purchase intent than Condition B because participants prioritize water‑saving features.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will show higher willingness to pay premium and higher purchase intent than Condition A because participants prioritize convenience and low‑maintenance features.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay premium in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., Condition A: 45% vs Condition B: 35%), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on water‑saving features. If Condition B exceeds Condition A by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience and low‑maintenance features. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, indicate uncertainty and recommend further market research.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Belimo Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current HVAC actuators, valves, and sensors, sold to commercial building manufacturers and through controls contractors and system integrators.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Any recommendation must consider Belimo’s existing B2B business model and current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., residential home automation, DIY HVAC control, or a new consumer segment).
2) Expand the existing B2B product portfolio with new features or packaging without targeting consumers directly.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial building manufacturers and system integrators.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct-to-consumer e‑commerce, partnerships with home‑im improvement retailers, or a subscription model for home control services).
5) Target a different customer group within the commercial segment (e.g., small‑to‑medium office buildings, residential building owners, or energy‑efficient retrofits).

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt Belimo residential control systems primarily to achieve energy savings and lower utility bills, and they will pay a premium for durable, low‑maintenance products that reduce HVAC system wear.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking to reduce energy costs and improve home comfort.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Energy‑awareness and cost‑saving incentives drive purchase decisions, and homeowners value products that minimize long‑term maintenance and repair costs.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Belimo can charge premium prices for energy‑efficient, durable products and capture value through higher margins and repeat purchases of replacement parts.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay more for energy‑efficient HVAC solutions.
Belimo's product quality and durability translate into lower long‑term ownership costs.
Regulatory incentives or utility rebates further motivate purchase.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate energy savings as the primary purchase driver.
Willingness to pay for a premium over standard HVAC actuators will be higher when energy‑efficiency benefits are emphasized.
Purchase intent will increase when presented with cost‑of‑ownership calculations showing lower utility bills over the product's lifetime.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt Belimo residential control systems primarily to achieve energy savings and lower utility bills, and they will pay a premium for durable, low‑maintenance products that reduce HVAC system wear.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt Belimo residential control systems primarily to gain home automation and smart home functionality, and they will pay a premium for integrated, app‑driven control that enhances convenience and connectivity.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners interested in smart home technology and convenience.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The growing demand for smart home ecosystems and the desire for seamless control of home devices drive purchase decisions, and homeowners seek products that can be managed remotely and integrated with other smart devices.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Belimo can capture value by offering integrated software platforms, app‑based control, and potential subscription services for home automation features, generating recurring revenue.
assumptions: Smart home adoption among homeowners is increasing.
Homeowners are willing to pay for integrated, app‑driven control features.
Belimo's technical capabilities can be leveraged to develop a consumer‑focused smart home platform.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate smart home functionality as the primary purchase driver.
Willingness to pay for a premium over standard HVAC actuators will be higher when smart home features are highlighted.
Purchase intent will increase when presented with scenarios showing remote control and integration with other smart devices.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Belimo Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current HVAC actuators, valves, and sensors, sold to commercial building manufacturers and through controls contractors and system integrators.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Any recommendation must consider Belimo’s existing B2B business model and current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., residential home automation, DIY HVAC control, or a new consumer segment).
2) Expand the existing B2B product portfolio with new features or packaging without targeting consumers directly.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial building manufacturers and system integrators.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct-to-consumer e‑commerce, partnerships with home‑im improvement retailers, or a subscription model for home control services).
5) Target a different customer group within the commercial segment (e.g., small‑to‑medium office buildings, residential building owners, or energy‑efficient retrofits).

T1.why_behaviour_changes: They will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition if they trust Belimo's reputation for durability and technical performance, and if the system offers clear ROI through reduced HVAC operation costs.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Belimo can capture value by selling premium‑priced residential control units directly to consumers through e‑commerce or retail partners, and by offering subscription services for monitoring and performance optimization.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for energy‑efficient HVAC control.
Belimo can deliver a product that integrates seamlessly with common residential HVAC systems.
There is sufficient consumer awareness of Belimo's existing commercial presence to justify a new consumer brand.
predictions: In a test offering a limited‑edition residential control kit at a 20% price premium over standard residential HVAC actuators, purchase intent among homeowners will exceed 15% among those who self‑identify as DIY homeowners.
Surveyed homeowners will rank energy‑efficiency and long‑term cost savings as the top two reasons for choosing a residential control system, above price or brand recognition.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Belimo Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current HVAC actuators, valves, and sensors, sold to commercial building manufacturers and through controls contractors and system integrators.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Any recommendation must consider Belimo’s existing B2B business model and current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., residential home automation, DIY HVAC control, or a new consumer segment).
2) Expand the existing B2B product portfolio with new features or packaging without targeting consumers directly.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial building manufacturers and system integrators.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct-to-consumer e‑commerce, partnerships with home‑im improvement retailers, or a subscription model for home control services).
5) Target a different customer group within the commercial segment (e.g., small‑to‑medium office buildings, residential building owners, or energy‑efficient retrofits).

T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking to lower energy costs and simplify HVAC control.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They switch from generic HVAC products to Belimo products when presented with clear cost‑of‑ownership benefits and technical credibility.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Belimo captures value through premium pricing, repeat purchases for additional accessories, and potential subscription revenue for monitoring services.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for energy‑efficient HVAC solutions.
Belimo can communicate cost savings and reliability effectively to consumers.
The market size for residential HVAC control is large enough to justify investment.
predictions: In a test offering a Belimo residential zone damper kit at a 15% premium over a generic equivalent, purchase intent will be at least 20% higher than for a generic kit.
Surveyed homeowners will rank cost savings and energy efficiency as top purchase drivers.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training that emphasizes personal safety, peace of mind, and convenience, rather than community or social responsibility. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium-priced home kit.

frame.objective: Determine whether Laerdal Medical should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current healthcare and training products, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage.
Investment must be justified by clear value capture mechanisms (e.g., premium pricing, subscription, or direct-to-consumer sales).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals).
2) Expand existing B2B products into new B2B segments (e.g., larger training organizations, hospitals).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current healthcare and training products for professionals.
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑brand or distribute existing products under a consumer brand.
5) License the core CPR technology to consumer electronics or lifestyle brands for consumer devices.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is marketed as a safety and peace-of-mind product, because they value personal protection and are willing to pay a premium for convenience and privacy.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers seeking personal health protection and peace of mind.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from viewing CPR training as a professional or institutional requirement to a personal responsibility when they perceive it as a low-risk, private activity that can be learned at any time.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal can capture value through premium-priced home kits, subscription-based access to training modules, and direct-to-consumer sales, leveraging its brand credibility in healthcare education.
assumptions: Consumers trust Laerdal's medical reputation to indicate safety.
Privacy and convenience are primary purchase drivers for home health products.
Willingness to pay exceeds cost of a standard CPR kit.
predictions: In a test offering a premium-priced home CPR kit, purchase intent among target consumers will be at least 20% higher than for a standard kit.
Surveyed consumers will rank 'peace of mind' as the top reason for choosing the home kit over a classroom or professional training.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is marketed as a safety and peace-of-mind product, because they value personal protection and are willing to pay a premium for convenience and privacy.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is positioned as a community or social responsibility, because they seek to contribute to public health and are motivated by peer influence and collective action.
T2.who_benefits: Individual consumers who feel a personal and social obligation to help others in cardiac emergencies.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from viewing CPR training as an individual responsibility to a collective one when they see it as part of a community effort, reducing perceived risk and increasing perceived social impact.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal can capture value through community-focused marketing, partnerships with schools, workplaces, and community organizations, and by offering group training programs that leverage shared responsibility.
assumptions: Consumers are motivated by social impact and community involvement.
Peer influence and collective action increase willingness to adopt health products.
Laerdal's brand can be associated with community health initiatives effectively.
predictions: In a test offering a community-focused home CPR kit, purchase intent among target consumers will be at least 15% higher than for a safety-focused kit.
Surveyed consumers will rank 'helping others' as the top reason for choosing the home kit over a personal peace-of-mind kit.

assessments.does_not_show: It does not demonstrate that consumers are willing to pay a premium for this convenience, nor that they perceive it as a safety or peace-of-mind product.

X1.name: Home CPR Kit Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer and randomized messaging variation.
X1.sample: 400 US adults recruited via an online panel, screened for interest in home health products and age 25-55.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and stated primary reason (safety/peace-of-mind vs community/social responsibility).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety/peace-of-mind messaging will generate purchase intent at least 20% higher than community messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Community/social responsibility messaging will generate purchase intent at least 20% higher than safety/peace-of-mind messaging.

X1.decision_rule: If safety/peace-of-mind messaging achieves purchase intent at least 20% higher than community messaging, recommend pursuing a consumer home CPR kit focused on personal protection. If community messaging achieves the higher rate, recommend a community-focused proposition. If neither meets the threshold, recommend no expansion.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training that emphasizes personal safety, peace of mind, and convenience, rather than community or social responsibility. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium-priced home kit.
final.target_customer: Individual consumers aged 25-55 who are interested in home health products and seek personal protection and convenience.
final.value_proposition: A portable, privacy-focused home CPR kit that allows learners to practice at their own pace, backed by Laerdal's medical credibility, offering peace of mind and convenience compared to classroom or professional training.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Home CPR Kit Messaging Test (400 US adults, €18,000, 10 weeks) to compare purchase intent for safety/peace-of-mind versus community messaging.
final.uncertainty: The willingness to pay for a premium-priced home kit is unknown; the test will determine whether consumers are willing to pay more than a standard kit. Additionally, the competitive landscape for home CPR products is unclear.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for safety/peace-of-mind messaging at least 20% higher than for community messaging, we would shift focus to a personal-protection proposition.
If the test shows neither messaging achieving the threshold, we would recommend no expansion and continue focusing on current B2B products.

frame.objective: Determine whether Laerdal Medical should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current healthcare and training products, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage.
Investment must be justified by clear value capture mechanisms (e.g., premium pricing, subscription, or direct-to-consumer sales).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals).
2) Expand existing B2B products into new B2B segments (e.g., larger training organizations, hospitals).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current healthcare and training products for professionals.
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑brand or distribute existing products under a consumer brand.
5) License the core CPR technology to consumer electronics or lifestyle brands for consumer devices.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if they view it as a personal health responsibility and a way to protect loved ones, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers who want to learn CPR for family emergencies.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Increased awareness of cardiac arrest statistics and personal risk perception motivates consumers to take proactive health measures.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal can charge a premium price for a consumer-friendly kit and potentially offer subscription-based access to updates and certification.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to invest time and money in learning CPR.
A consumer brand can effectively communicate the health benefit and safety of the product.
Regulatory and insurance requirements will not significantly increase the cost of consumer CPR training.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate high intent to purchase a home CPR kit within the next 12 months.
Willingness to pay will be above the current price point of Laerdal's existing consumer kits (estimated €50-€100).
Purchase decisions will be driven by perceived personal benefit rather than professional certification.

X1.name: Family vs Personal Health Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults (n=400). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A receives a personal health message emphasizing the consumer benefits of learning CPR for family emergencies (e.g., 'Protect your family by learning CPR at home'). Condition B receives a family-friendly message emphasizing shared learning and bonding (e.g., 'Teach your family CPR together and create quality family time'). Both conditions present the same product (Laerdal CPR Anytime home training kit). Participants are asked to report purchase intent (1-7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 400 adults aged 18-65, screened for interest in home CPR training.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (1-7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Condition B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Condition A.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between Condition A and Condition B is >= 1.5 points, we conclude that personal health messaging (T1) is more effective. If the difference is <= 1.5 points, we conclude that family-friendly messaging (T2) is more effective. If both conditions show similar intent, we recommend further testing.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals) that emphasizes personal health responsibility and family protection. Begin with a low-cost online survey test to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling.
final.target_customer: Individual consumers aged 18-65 who want to learn CPR for family emergencies.
final.value_proposition: A portable, easy-to-share home CPR kit that empowers consumers to protect their families, offering a premium price point and optional subscription for updates and certification.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Family vs Personal Health Messaging Test (400 adults, 6 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under personal health vs family-friendly messaging.
final.uncertainty: The actual demand for consumer CPR training is unknown; willingness to pay may be lower than expected, and competitive positioning could affect acceptance.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 1.5 points relative to a control condition, we would reconsider the investment.
If a separate test shows strong demand for family-friendly messaging, we would shift focus to a family-oriented proposition.
If willingness to pay is significantly lower than €50-€100, we would explore lower-priced or subscription models.

frame.objective: Determine whether Laerdal Medical should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current healthcare and training products, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage.
Investment must be justified by clear value capture mechanisms (e.g., premium pricing, subscription, or direct-to-consumer sales).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals).
2) Expand existing B2B products into new B2B segments (e.g., larger training organizations, hospitals).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current healthcare and training products for professionals.
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑brand or distribute existing products under a consumer brand.
5) License the core CPR technology to consumer electronics or lifestyle brands for consumer devices.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is marketed as a safety and peace-of-mind product for families, because they view CPR as a life-saving skill they should be prepared to perform.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners and their families who want to be ready for a medical emergency.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The perceived risk of a cardiac arrest in the home increases when the threat is real, and the desire to protect loved ones motivates purchase of a product that provides immediate, easy-to-learn training.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal can capture value through premium pricing for a consumer-friendly kit, subscription for ongoing content, and direct-to-consumer sales that leverage existing distribution channels.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product marketed as a safety solution.
Marketing can effectively communicate the life-saving benefits of home CPR training.
Distribution channels can reach individual buyers without significant cost.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer-focused home CPR kit, purchase intent will be higher than for a professional training kit.
Willingness to pay will be above the cost of a standard CPR mannequin, indicating a premium market.
Adoption will be higher in households with children or elderly members who are more likely to face home emergencies.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is marketed as a safety and peace-of-mind product for families, because they view CPR as a life-saving skill they should be prepared to perform.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is positioned as a health insurance requirement or a workplace wellness program, because they view it as a mandatory or incentivized health commitment.
T2.who_benefits: Insurance companies, employers, and individual policyholders who seek to meet regulatory or wellness requirements.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Mandatory or incentivized training reduces perceived risk and creates a structured learning path, making purchase more likely than voluntary adoption.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal can capture value through bulk licensing to insurance providers and employers, subscription for compliance reporting, and direct-to-consumer sales bundled with insurance or HR packages.
assumptions: Insurance and workplace wellness programs influence consumer purchasing decisions.
Regulatory requirements for CPR training exist in target markets.
Laerdal can secure partnerships to integrate its products into existing compliance programs.
predictions: In a test offering a home CPR kit as part of an insurance or workplace wellness program, purchase intent will be higher than for a standalone consumer kit.
Willingness to pay will be lower than for a premium consumer kit, reflecting cost-sharing.
Adoption will be higher among households with children or elderly members who face higher health risks.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test
X1.method: Randomized controlled trial with two groups receiving a home CPR kit. Group A receives a consumer-focused kit marketed as a safety and peace-of-mind product for families. Group B receives the same kit but marketed as part of an insurance or workplace wellness program. Both groups are offered a small refundable deposit to confirm interest. The test is run online with a survey to measure purchase intent, willingness to pay, and stated motivation.
X1.sample: 300 adult participants recruited via an online panel, split evenly between Group A and Group B.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy), willingness to pay (USD), and stated motivation (safety vs. insurance/workplace wellness).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B, because safety and peace-of-mind drive consumer adoption.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A, because insurance or workplace wellness requirements motivate purchase.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A purchase intent exceeds Group B by at least 10 percentage points and willingness to pay is at least 20% higher, proceed with a consumer proposition focused on safety. If Group B exceeds Group A by at least 10 percentage points and willingness to pay is at least 20% higher, pursue an insurance/workplace wellness positioning. If neither difference meets the thresholds, do not invest in this proposition.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training, focusing on safety and peace-of-mind positioning. The evidence shows Laerdal already offers a consumer-friendly home program and that bystander CPR rates are increasing, suggesting a market opportunity. The proposed test should be run to validate whether safety-driven motivation drives higher purchase intent than insurance/workplace wellness.
final.target_customer: Individual homeowners and their families who want to be prepared for home emergencies.
final.value_proposition: A home CPR kit marketed as a safety and peace-of-mind product, offering flexible, private training that can be shared with family members, providing immediate, easy-to-learn lifesaving skills.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test (300 participants, two randomized groups, refundable deposit, purchase intent and willingness to pay survey) to determine whether safety-driven motivation drives higher adoption than insurance/work
final.uncertainty: Actual purchase behavior and willingness to pay are unknown; the test will resolve this. Also uncertain is the extent to which insurance or workplace wellness requirements influence consumer decisions.
would_change_if: If the test shows Group B (insurance/workplace wellness positioning) achieving higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A, the recommendation would shift to pursue an insurance/workplace wellness proposition.
If the test fails to meet the thresholds for either safety or insurance/workplace positioning, the investment would be reconsidered or the proposition would be abandoned.

frame.objective: Determine whether Laerdal Medical should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current healthcare and training products, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners and their families who want to be prepared for cardiac emergencies.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of cardiac arrest frequency and the role of bystanders (supported by data on bystander CPR rates increasing) creates a perceived need for home preparedness.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal can sell premium-priced home training kits directly to consumers, generate recurring revenue through optional add-ons (e.g., family training modules) and subscription services for updates.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that can save lives.
Home CPR training is perceived as accessible and easy to learn.
Regulatory or insurance incentives (e.g., coverage for home training) would increase adoption.
predictions: A survey of homeowners would show >30% intent to purchase a home CPR kit at a price point above $50.
Sales of a consumer-facing home CPR kit would increase in regions with higher public awareness of cardiac arrest.
Repeat purchase rate for optional training modules would be higher than for a one-time purchase.

assumptions: Insurance and employer coverage requirements for CPR training exist and are enforceable.
Consumers are willing to purchase training kits to meet these requirements.
Laerdal can secure partnerships with insurers and HR departments to promote the product.
predictions: Insurance or employer-sponsored home CPR training programs would show higher adoption rates than consumer-led initiatives.
Sales would be concentrated in regions with strict coverage requirements for CPR training.
Customers would be more likely to purchase kits when presented with compliance-related messaging.

X1.name: Consumer vs Compliance Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a description of a home CPR training kit and are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑2 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR). They are then asked about their primary reason for purchase (personal preparedness, insurance/employer requirement, or other).
X1.sample: 400 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced across two conditions: 200 see personal preparedness messaging and 200 see compliance messaging.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (1‑2 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: reason for purchase (open-ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the personal preparedness condition compared to the compliance condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the compliance condition compared to the personal preparedness condition.

X1.decision_rule: If personal preparedness messaging yields purchase intent at least 10 points higher than compliance messaging (e.g., mean intent 1.5 vs 1.0), recommend developing a consumer proposition focused on personal preparedness. If compliance messaging yields purchase intent at least 10 points higher, recommend a compliance‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is <5 points, indicate uncertainty and suggest further market research.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer demand for home CPR training, personal preparedness, or compliance messaging. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training, focusing on personal preparedness messaging. Begin with a small-scale pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay, and use the results to decide on pricing and distribution.
final.target_customer: Individual homeowners and their families who want to be prepared for cardiac emergencies.
final.value_proposition: A home CPR training kit that empowers families to perform CPR in emergencies, leveraging Laerdal’s expertise to provide a safe, easy-to-learn solution that can save lives.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Compliance Messaging Test (400 U.S. adults, 8 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under personal preparedness vs. compliance messaging.
final.uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for a home CPR kit and the size of the consumer market remain uncertain. Evidence of strong demand is limited to market facts about home cardiac arrests, not to consumer purchase behavior.
would_change_if: If the pilot shows purchase intent below 20% or willingness to pay below €50, indicating low consumer demand, the recommendation would shift toward no expansion or a different route to market.
If compliance messaging yields purchase intent at least 10 points higher than personal preparedness messaging, the recommendation would shift toward a compliance-focused consumer proposition.

X1.name: Family vs Mandate Purchase Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two scenarios: Family Sharing (premium-priced kit marketed as a family safety product that can be shared among relatives and friends) or Mandate (premium-priced kit marketed as a health insurance or employer mandate requirement). Both scenarios include a brief description of the kit and a price point. Participants indicate whether they would purchase the kit and, if so, the primary reason (family sharing vs mandate).
X1.sample: 500 homeowners aged 25-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and primary reason for purchase (family sharing vs mandate).

prediction_by_theory.T1: In the Family Sharing scenario, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than in the Mandate scenario.
prediction_by_theory.T2: In the Mandate scenario, purchase intent will be at least 20% higher than in the Family Sharing scenario.

X1.decision_rule: If Family Sharing purchase intent ≥ 15% and Mandate purchase intent ≤ 20%, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition for family sharing. If Mandate purchase intent ≥ 20% and Family Sharing purchase intent ≤ 15%, proceed with a mandate-compliant consumer proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer market.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer purchase motivations for home CPR training. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for family sharing, but first validate demand through a low-cost purchase intent test. If the test meets the Family Sharing threshold, proceed with a premium-priced family-sharing kit; otherwise, do not expand into consumer market.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and their families who are interested in learning CPR and want to train together as a shared responsibility.
final.value_proposition: A portable, family-sharing CPR kit that allows multiple family members to learn CPR together, reducing perceived risk and increasing confidence to respond to cardiac arrest.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Family vs Mandate Purchase Test (500 homeowners, 8 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent under family-sharing vs mandate scenarios.
final.uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for a family-sharing kit and the size of the market remain uncertain. Evidence shows Laerdal already sells a consumer kit (Mini Anne) but does not show it is purchased for family sharing.
would_change_if: If the Family Sharing purchase intent threshold is not met (e.g., <15%), the recommendation would shift to not expand into consumer market.

arguments.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is marketed as a family safety product that can be shared among relatives and friends, because they view CPR as a mutual responsibility and need to be trained together.
arguments.who_benefits: Homeowners and their families gain confidence and ability to respond to cardiac arrest; Laerdal gains volume sales and brand extension.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: A shift from viewing CPR training as a professional-only requirement to a shared family responsibility reduces perceived risk and increases willingness to invest in training together.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal sells kits directly to consumers at a premium price and can offer subscription or bundle services for family training sessions.
assumptions: Consumers trust Laerdal's medical credibility to deliver effective training.

Regulatory or insurance incentives do not yet require home training.
predictions: In a test offering a family-sharing kit at a premium price, purchase intent among homeowners will be at least 15% higher than a single-user kit.
Surveyed homeowners will cite 'training with family' as the top reason for choosing the product over a professional-only kit.

arguments.name: Family vs Mandate Purchase Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two scenarios: Family Sharing (premium-priced kit marketed as a family safety product that can be shared among relatives and friends) or Mandate (premium-priced kit marketed as a health insurance or employer mandate requirement). Both scenarios include a brief description of the kit and a price point. Participants indicate whether they would purchase the kit and, if so, the primary reason (family sharing vs mandate).
arguments.sample: 500 homeowners aged 25-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and primary reason for purchase (family sharing vs mandate).

prediction_by_theory.T1: In the Family Sharing scenario, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than in the Mandate scenario.
prediction_by_theory.T2: In the Mandate scenario, purchase intent will be at least 20% higher than in the Family Sharing scenario.

arguments.decision_rule: If Family Sharing purchase intent ≥ 15% and Mandate purchase intent ≤ 20%, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition for family sharing. If Mandate purchase intent ≥ 20% and Family Sharing purchase intent ≤ 15%, proceed with a mandate-compliant consumer proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer market.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for family sharing, but first validate demand through a low-cost purchase intent test. If the test meets the Family Sharing threshold, proceed with a premium-priced family-sharing kit; otherwise, do not expand into consumer market.

frame.objective: Determine whether Laerdal Medical should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current healthcare and training products, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage.
Investment must be justified by clear value capture mechanisms (e.g., premium pricing, subscription, or direct-to-consumer sales).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals).
2) Expand existing B2B products into new B2B segments (e.g., larger training organizations, hospitals).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current healthcare and training products for professionals.
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑brand or distribute existing products under a consumer brand.
5) License the core CPR technology to consumer electronics or lifestyle brands for consumer devices.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is marketed as a safety and preparedness product for families, because they view CPR as a life-saving skill they should learn before an emergency occurs.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners and their families who want to be prepared for cardiac arrest.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The perceived threat of cardiac arrest and the desire to protect loved ones motivates purchase of a home training kit.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal can sell premium-priced home kits directly to consumers, capture recurring revenue through optional add-ons (e.g., family training sessions), and build a subscription model for updates.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product marketed as life-saving.
Marketing can effectively communicate the safety and preparedness benefits.
Distribution channels (e.g., online, retail) can reach target consumers.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate intent to purchase a home CPR kit at a price above $100.
Sales of home kits will increase in regions with higher reported cardiac arrest incidence.
Repeat purchase rate for optional training sessions will be higher than for a one-time purchase.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is marketed as a safety and preparedness product for families, because they view CPR as a life-saving skill they should learn before an emergency occurs.

The survey measures purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum price willing to pay.

X1.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of respondents indicating "would buy" for each price point) and maximum price willing to pay.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay at the premium price compared to Group B.

If neither threshold is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting DIY homeowners, leveraging Kingspan’s existing direct‑to‑consumer sales channel and energy‑efficiency messaging. Begin with a limited pilot of a consumer‑focused hub offering DIY kits and installation guides, using the proposed test to validate purchase intent and professional‑installation preference before scaling.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Kingspan Group plc investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B insulation and building envelope products.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Need to identify existing consumer reach (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales, retail partnerships) and demand for a differentiated product.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer willingness to purchase, current market size, and potential value capture for Kingspan.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., homeowner DIY insulation, small‑scale building retrofits).
2) Expand the existing B2B insulation and building envelope products into new professional segments (e.g., larger construction firms, public‑building contractors).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market without introducing a consumer proposition.
4) Partner with existing consumer brands or retailers to bring Kingspan products to individual buyers (e.g., retail distribution of insulation panels).
5) License the insulation technology to consumer‑focused manufacturers rather than selling under the Kingspan brand.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Kingspan can sell through its own website or a dedicated consumer hub at premium prices, capturing value through direct sales rather than relying on distributors.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to purchase insulation products online and follow DIY installation guides.

Energy‑efficiency incentives remain active in target markets.
predictions: A survey of homeowners in target markets will show >50% indicating intent to purchase insulation for energy savings.

Return rates for DIY kits will be lower than for professional‑delivered products.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase and installation choice. Participants are recruited from UK homeowners who have completed a home energy audit. They view a product description of Kingspan Kooltherm insulation and are presented with two options: (1) purchase a DIY kit with installation instructions and delivery, or (2) book a professional installation through a partner. They are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and whether they would choose professional installation (yes/no).
X1.sample: 400 UK homeowners who have completed a home energy audit, recruited via an online panel. Stratified by region and income to reflect diverse market segments.
X1.measure: Primary measure: purchase intent score (1‑10) for each option. Secondary measure: binary choice of whether they would choose professional installation versus DIY.

prediction_by_theory.T1: DIY purchase intent will be higher than professional installation intent, and the difference will be statistically significant (p<0.05).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Professional installation intent will be higher than DIY purchase intent, and the difference will be statistically significant (p<0.05).

X1.decision_rule: If DIY purchase intent ≥ 55 and professional installation intent ≤ 45, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting DIY homeowners. If professional installation intent ≥ 55 and DIY purchase intent ≤ 45, pursue professional installation as the primary consumer proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer sales.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Kingspan Group plc investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B insulation and building envelope products.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Need to identify existing consumer reach (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales, retail partnerships) and demand for a differentiated product.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer willingness to purchase, current market size, and potential value capture for Kingspan.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., homeowner DIY insulation, small‑scale building retrofits).
2) Expand the existing B2B insulation and building envelope products into new professional segments (e.g., larger construction firms, public‑building contractors).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market without introducing a consumer proposition.
4) Partner with existing consumer brands or retailers to bring Kingspan products to individual buyers (e.g., retail distribution of insulation panels).
5) License the insulation technology to consumer‑focused manufacturers rather than selling under the Kingspan brand.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt Kingspan insulation if they perceive it as a reliable, government‑approved solution for energy efficiency, because they trust public funding (SEAI grants) and regulatory requirements.
T1.who_benefits: Kingspan gains volume sales and brand association with public energy‑efficiency programs.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: When homeowners receive SEAI grants or must meet building codes, they choose products that simplify the grant application and project management, reducing DIY risk.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kingspan sells through the Insulation One Stop Shop model, capturing margin on products and service fees, and can bundle grants with installation.
assumptions: SEAI grants and building codes are actively promoted to homeowners.
Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for a product that simplifies the grant process.
Kingspan can scale the One Stop Shop model to reach a large segment of homeowners.
predictions: In regions with active SEAI grant programs, homeowner purchase intent for Kingspan will be higher than for competitors.
Homeowners will report lower perceived risk when choosing Kingspan due to the simplified grant process.
Sales growth will be driven by the number of grants issued, not just individual purchases.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt Kingspan insulation if they perceive it as a reliable, government‑approved solution for energy efficiency, because they trust public funding (SEAI grants) and regulatory requirements.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt Kingspan insulation if they perceive it as a premium, high‑performance product that offers superior thermal efficiency and durability, because they value long‑term value and are willing to pay a premium for quality.
T2.who_benefits: Kingspan gains higher‑margin sales and can position itself as a premium brand in the insulation market.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: When homeowners compare insulation products, they choose the one they believe will provide the best energy‑efficiency and lifespan, even if it costs more.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Kingspan can price its premium product at a higher margin and sell through specialized channels or direct‑to‑consumer platforms, capturing value through brand differentiation.
assumptions: Homeowners have the financial means to purchase premium insulation.
The premium product is differentiated by thermal performance and durability.
Marketing can effectively communicate the premium value to homeowners.
predictions: In markets where energy‑efficiency is a primary purchase driver, homeowners will show higher willingness to pay for Kingspan's premium product.
Homeowners will report higher satisfaction with the product's performance compared to competitors.
Sales of the premium product will be concentrated in regions where energy‑efficiency is a key purchase criterion.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Kingspan Group plc investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B insulation and building envelope products.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Need to identify existing consumer reach (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales, retail partnerships) and demand for a differentiated product.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer willingness to purchase, current market size, and potential value capture for Kingspan.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., homeowner DIY insulation, small‑scale building retrofits).
2) Expand the existing B2B insulation and building envelope products into new professional segments (e.g., larger construction firms, public‑building contractors).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market without introducing a consumer proposition.
4) Partner with existing consumer brands or retailers to bring Kingspan products to individual buyers (e.g., retail distribution of insulation panels).
5) License the insulation technology to consumer‑focused manufacturers rather than selling under the Kingspan brand.

X1.name: Digital Messaging Test: SEAI vs Premium Messaging
X1.method: Run a targeted online survey with two equal arms: Arm A receives a message emphasizing SEAI grant support and the One Stop Shop process; Arm B receives a message emphasizing premium thermal performance and durability. Both arms include a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question. Recruit 500 homeowners in the UK who have shown interest in home insulation (via a pre‐screen). Randomly assign participants to either Arm A or Arm B, then collect responses to the WTP question.
X1.sample: 500 homeowners in the UK who have shown interest in home insulation (pre‐screen).
X1.measure: Willingness-to-pay (WTP) for Kingspan's product, measured in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A will show a significantly higher WTP than Arm B, because homeowners trust the grant process and are motivated by public funding.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B will show a significantly higher WTP than Arm A, because homeowners value premium performance and are willing to pay more for superior thermal efficiency.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP in Arm A is at least 20% higher than in Arm B, proceed with developing a consumer proposition that emphasizes SEAI grant support (supporting T1). If Arm B's WTP is at least 20% higher than Arm A, proceed with a premium positioning (supporting T2). If the difference is less than 20% or both arms are equal, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows Kingspan already sells directly to end-users and offers a One Stop Shop for SEAI grants, but it does not demonstrate that homeowners are aware of or actively seeking grants to drive purchase. A targeted digital test (e.g., SEAI vs premium messaging) is needed to validate willingness-to-pay before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Homeowners in the UK who are interested in home insulation and may be eligible for SEAI grants, as identified by the One Stop Shop model.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that either leverages the existing SEAI One Stop Shop process (supporting T1) or emphasizes premium thermal performance and durability (supporting T2), with a clear willingness-to-pay mechanism.
final.next_action: Run the proposed digital messaging test (SEAI vs premium messaging) to measure willingness-to-pay and decide whether to proceed with a consumer proposition based on the results.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, the actual willingness-to-pay for Kingspan's products, and the extent to which homeowners are aware of or actively seek SEAI grants are uncertain.
would_change_if: If the test shows a willingness-to-pay difference of at least 20% between SEAI and premium messaging, we would proceed with a consumer proposition that emphasizes the grant process (supporting T1).
If the test shows a willingness-to-pay difference of at least 20% in favor of premium positioning, we would proceed with a premium positioning strategy (supporting T2).

X1.name: Digital Messaging Test: Grant vs Cost‑Effective Messaging
X1.method: Run a targeted online survey with two parallel messaging groups. Group A sees a message emphasizing government‑approved energy‑efficiency certification and SEAI grant eligibility. Group B sees a message emphasizing long‑term cost savings and reduced future heating bills. Both groups view a product description of Kingspan's 270mm rigid insulation board. Recruit 500 homeowners in the UK who have completed a home energy audit or are considering retrofitting.
X1.sample: 500 UK homeowners who have completed a home energy audit or are considering retrofitting.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured as a binary choice: "Would you purchase this insulation product?" and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Group B, because homeowners are motivated by grant eligibility and government certification.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Group A, because homeowners prioritize long‑term cost savings and energy bill reduction.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for Group A is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A ≥ 65% and Group B ≤ 50%), proceed to develop a consumer proposition focused on grant‑eligibility messaging. If Group B is at least 15 percentage points higher, develop a cost‑effective messaging proposition. If neither difference is statistically significant (p ≥ 0.05), do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes government‑approved energy‑efficiency certification and SEAI grant eligibility, rather than a cost‑effective messaging approach. final.value_proposition: A certified, grant‑eligible insulation product that simplifies the retrofit process and delivers measurable energy‑efficiency savings, positioned as a trusted, government‑approved solution.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Digital Messaging Test (or a smaller pilot) to validate purchase intent differences between grant‑eligibility and cost‑effective messaging, using the 15‑percentage‑point threshold.
final.uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for certified products and the extent to which homeowners actively seek grants remain uncertain; the test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows no significant difference in purchase intent between the two messaging groups (p ≥ 0.05), the recommendation would shift to a cost‑effective proposition.
If new evidence shows that homeowners do not trust government certification or are unlikely to apply for grants, T1 would become less likely and the strategy would need to be adjusted.

Participants are randomly assigned to one of the two descriptions and asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent on a 7-point scale. A control group receives a neutral description.
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced between outdoor recreation and non-recreation segments.
X1.measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) in euros for the specialized glove, and purchase intent on a 7-point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants exposed to the specialized, premium description will have a WTP at least 20% higher and purchase intent at least 15% higher than those exposed to the neutral description.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants exposed to the specialized, premium description will have a WTP at least 20% higher and purchase intent at least 15% higher than those exposed to the neutral description.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for the specialized description exceeds the neutral description by at least 20% AND the purchase intent for the specialized description exceeds the neutral description by at least 15%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 20% for either WTP or purchase intent, do not invest in a differentiated proposition.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation) that emphasizes premium design, superior protection, and style. Begin with a small-scale pilot test to validate consumer willingness to pay and purchase intent before scaling.

final.value_proposition: A purpose-built, stylish protective glove that offers enhanced protection and durability, positioned as a premium item that combines functionality with aesthetic appeal.

final.uncertainty: The exact size of the consumer market for differentiated protective gloves and the willingness to pay a premium are uncertain. Additionally, the competitive landscape and Ansell's ability to differentiate in a crowded market are unknown.
would_change_if: If the pilot test shows a willingness to pay difference of less than 20% or purchase intent difference of less than 15% between the specialized and neutral descriptions, the investment would be reconsidered in favor of no expansion.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt differentiated protective gloves for specific use cases (e.g., outdoor recreation, cycling, gardening) if they perceive the product as a premium, specialized item that offers superior protection and style, leading to higher willingness to pay and repeat purchases.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers seeking specialized protection for activities where standard gloves fail.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Shifting from generic industrial gloves to purpose-built, stylish gloves creates a perceived value that justifies higher price and multiple purchases.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can capture value through premium pricing, brand differentiation, and potential licensing of the specialized design to third-party consumer brands.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for specialized protective gear.
The differentiated product can be produced at scale without compromising quality.
The brand can be effectively positioned as premium and specialized in the consumer market.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a specialized glove compared to standard industrial gloves.
Purchase intent for the specialized glove will be higher among consumers who engage in outdoor activities than among those who do not.
Repeat purchase rate for the specialized glove will be higher than for standard industrial gloves.
